Objectives: ...using prescribed burning to reduce sagebrush density on sagebrush/grassland vegetation types throughout the Bates Creek allotment.
Planned_Implementation: Under the proposed action, a schedule of fall burn treatments will be initiated under the current rest-rotation grazing system. Each pasture will be scheduled for prescribed burning at a time when the rotation sequence will allow 18 to 20 months of rest from livestock grazing after the fall burn treatment. The stages of implementation of the proposed action are outlined in the "Prescribed Burning Plan for Bates Creek Pasture, Fall Burn #1, 1982&&.
Actual_Implementation:
The fire burned, as predicted, in heavy patches and stringers of sagebrush and went out or failed to carry in
thinner areas. Even with temperature of 78 degrees and RH of 22% the fire would not carry across marginal areas without wind speeds of 15 mph or more. Test burning was conducted under the latter conditions to see if and how fire would carry in the marginal areas. A higher amount of fine fuels must also be present for fire to carry in marginal areas. Very little
preparation was necessary to keep the burn confined to the treatment area. Some blacklining was employed the first day
to confine burning to one block; the blacklining was only partially successful and in reality not necessary. Blacklining
was employed along a fenceline on the south side of the treatment pasture to protect the fenceline and prevent fire from spreading to another pasture. These latter efforts were successful.
All firing was done by hand (drip torch) using strip-head fire and headfire techniques.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
The current community structure and composition depict unhealthy, decadent
ponderosa pine trees/stands and are altering traditional ecological processes found in
ponderosa pine communities. High tree density increases growth rate variability and thus
drastically decreases seed production that influences future ponderosa pine rejuvenation.
Additionally, increased tree density reduces shrub and herbaceous cover through interspecific
competition. This results in accelerated soil erosion, increased sediment loads in waterways
and reduced site potential.

Pinyon and juniper have extremely high evapotranspiration and interception rates and can
maintain a competitive advantage for precipitation over other species. Therefore,
pinyon/juniper invasion greatly influences the hydrologic cycle. Research shows a 6.5 inch
diameter at breast height (dbh) juniper would use .089 inches of precipitation annually. A
site with 100 trees per acre would lose 8.9 inches of precipitation and 250 trees per acre
would consume 22.3 inches of precipitation annually.

Most important, excessive tree density coupled with decadence due to retarded tree growth
and disease infestation (i.e., mistletoe) create a structural stand integrity conducive to
catastrophic fire. The high tree density coupled with stagnant growth provides a close net in
the canopy and structural ladder fuels to facilitate canopy crown fires. The high intensity and
high severity nature of a stand replacing crown fire could result in drastic community
composition changes and severe soil loss. Catastrophic fires also threaten the lives and
property of people in the area.

Objectives:
The objectives of the burn are to reduce fuel accumulations on public lands, thus reducing the threat of a
wildfire getting established and becoming catastrophic and moving from BLM to private land. This burn is
also a wildlife burn to provide deer and elk with better habitat. This area is a critical winter range for deer
and elk. The Colorado Department of Wildlife is a cooperator in this project. This burn will help create
better forage for deer and elk throughout the winter months, reducing wildlife impacts to private lands and
roadways.
Planned_Implementation:
Control lines for this project are as follows. The north boW1dary is adjacent to a hydro-axe W1it that will
serve as a good fuel break. Hand lines will be put in if necessary prior to burn day. The east boundary of
the project is a ridge line where the backside (east) of the ridge is sparse with fuel. A control line has
already been placed along the ridge in fall of2008. The south side of the unit bounded by BLM road 8334.
This road will serve as a very good fuel break/fire line. The west boundary is BLM road 8334 also. Once
again this road is a very good fuel break for the unit.
The unit will be hand ignited using drip torches or other ignition devices such as fusees and quoin guns.
There will be smoke information signs posted along the East Sopris Road and Highway 82 to inform the
public of the burning activity in the area.
Actual_Implementation:
During this burn we encountered very few issues that hindered the
operation or the success of the project. Ignition rates were slowed down for the entire unit due to the East black lining operation. Ignitions were slow here due to shading/ steep slopes. After
looking at fire behavior and depth of the blackline along the east side, the ridge top would have
been enough to hold the fire without black line. Another piece of unit preparation which
slowed ignition just slightly was hand line along the west line to cut off the switch back corners.
1/2 day of prep could resolve this issue in the future.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
On all of the objectives listed, the burn was very successful. Top kill in the oak was very
successful with approximately 60-75% of the oak within the unit being top killed, and 90% of
the P&J consumed. This success can be attributed to burning under conditions that would
resemble a natural wildfire event. Great job by the personnel on scene.

Objectives:
The overall objective of the burn is to stimulate the sprouting of oak brush, rejuvenate browse species such as snowberry and
mahogany, and re-establish herbaceous species. Accomplishment of this objective will
result in the following:
• Improve overall wildlife habitat diversity.
• Improve quality and quantity of available winter forage for elk, pronghorn, and
mule deer.
• Reduce elk, pronghorn, and mule deer foraging energy expenditure during severe
weather conditions.
• Improve overall vigor and productivity of game herds.
• Allow for maximum herd growth to optimize hunting opportunity as well as nonconsumptive
recreational uses.
Planned_Implementation:
A burn plan will be prepared to determine and prescribe the conditions under which the
burn can be initiated and conducted. The objective is to conduct a spring burn if possible.
The treatment should be conducted as soon as the area meets prescription, fuels are dry enough to carry the fire, and before extensive green up. Preferred dates are between early
April and late May. If conditions in the spring are not conducive to burning then the
treatment may be done in the fall, dates of the burn determined by weather and fuel
conditions.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
In 1988, the Taos Field Office conducted a prescribed burn on BLM lands located on the
northeastern slope of San Antonio Mountain. This burn was done to compliment a range
improvement prescribed fire conducted by the U.S. Forest Service and the Rocky
Mountain Elk Foundation on the south side of San Antonio Mountain in 1987. The
objective of both the USFS and BLM burns was to stimulate and regenerate decadent oak
brush growth to support year-round range requirements of the area&$s resident and
migratory herds of elk, pronghorn, and mule deer.

The Taos Field Office BLM is now proposing a &&maintenance&& prescribed burn in the
same area, intended to stimulate sprouting of oak brush, rejuvenate browse species such
as snowberry and mahogany, and re-establish herbaceous species. The purpose of this
Environmental Assessment is to re-evaluate impacts of the proposed action which were
previously addressed in the original San Antonio Mountain Burn EA# NM-018-88-08.

Objectives:
Improve wildlife habitat by increasing structural and age class diversity of the shrub species in the target area.
Create a mosaic of burned/unburned vegetation to increase “edge” effect in Pinyon-Juniper and mountain shrub Communities in the overall Eagle Valley Project area.  Decrease short-term large wildland fire hazard by reducing fuel loadings.
Reduce fire danger to adjacent private property.
Remove 40-90% of Pinon-Juniper in treatment area.
 40-80% of sagebrush can be black or burnt, a mosaic pattern will be desired to aid in post fire recolonization
 Reintroduce fire into fire adapted community. Maintain at least 2 foot average flame length during periods of active ignition. 
Achieve black line depth adequate for the expected weather conditions and fire behavior with relation to
fuels and objectives of this project. Contain slop-overs or spot fires as quickly as possible or by the end burn period. Provide for safe and effective use of all personnel associated with this project.
Planned_Implementation:
Based on forecasted wind direction, fuels and topography a location will be selected for a test fire in a suitable area. Test fire will be documented by Burn Boss and submitted with the Burn Boss Report. Test fire will be at a location that is easily controllable if results are undesirable. One drip torch will be used to start a small strip head fire. The Burn Boss may wish to ignite more than one test fire in different locations in other representative fuel types to determine conditions. Firing Methods:
FIRING: Test fire will be conducted to assess fire behavior predictions and validity of prescription parameters. Ignition will not take place if prescriptive parameters are exceeded. Results of each test fire will be documented. Different firing patterns will be used dependent of topography, fuels and wind and fire behavior to meet objectives. The Burn Boss/ Ignitions Specialist/Holding Specialist will select the best firing pattern(s) that will meet objectives, provide for safety and minimize the potential for escape.
TECHNIQUES: Strip head firing is planned for the main portions of the Units. Some slower, less aggressive black lining will be necessary at the beginning phases of each Unit as well as flanking strips or dot ignition may be used as well. Needed depth of the black lining will be determined by fuel moisture conditions, predicted weather for the days and observed fire behavior.
SEQUENCES: Exact sequence(s) of ignition will be determined by RXB2, FIRB, and Holding Specialist on day(s) of active ignitions on this project. The anticipated sequences will be from upslope proceeding downslope as well as into the days forecasted winds and observed winds to provide for safety and minimize the potential for escape.
ANTICIPATED PATTERNS: A variety of patterns may be used to meet objectives. It is anticipated that strip head firing will be the primary ignition method strips will vary in width as long as fuels are continuous and will grow together to meet objectives. Actual patterns, sequences, etc. will be determined based on weather and fuel conditions on the day(s) of burning.
IGNITION STAFFING: Ignition personnel and makeup will be determined by the Burn Boss and FIRB with considerations of anticipated desired fire behavior for each Unit. One or two groups of five personnel should be adequate for ground ignition operations. Spring time burning will not require as large of staff and can be determined by the burn boss on the day of the burn.
Good communications between ignition and holding forces will need to be maintained throughout all ignition operations. This will mitigate potential problems resulting from ignitions proceeding faster than holding actions can be accomplished. Lighters should be able to see each other much of the time, but must always be able to hear each other.
Devices:
Ground based firing devices will include but are not limited to drip torch, fusee, terra-torch and quoin-gun if necessary. Minimum Ignition Staffing:
For Fall burning a minimum ignition crew of 5 people is necessary 1 firing boss and 4 lighters.
For Spring burning a minimum ignition crew of 3 people is necessary 1 firing boss and 2 lighters which is slightly different from the fall ignition organization. Prescribed fire will be called out no less than 2 days after the last smoke has been observed and then only at the burn bosses discretion. Burn Boss Report will be prepared at the end of each operational day. The report will be kept in the Burn plan folder and submitted for the project file. It will include conditions encountered during implementation, pertinent weather and fuels conditions and any unexpected fire behavior. Results as compared to desired objectives of the burn will be documented and any pictures that would be useful to document fire behavior. Monitoring conducted to compare fire treatment objectives and resource objective that were identified in the project will be kept both in the burn plan folder and the project file Smoke dispersal will be addressed, as will any actions taken in relation to residences in the area or traffic along I-70. Permanent photo points can be established within the project area. Vegetation monitoring using Rapid Assessment non-permanent plots could also be utilized. Daily “actual accomplishment” reports will be submitted to Air Pollution Control Division as per smoke permit requirements. Accomplishments will be recorded in NFPORS after the fire is declared out.

Trt_Concerns_Desc: Based on past experience in similar fuels and topography, flame lengths will need to be sustained at an average of 2 feet or greater head fire in the SH7 fuel model to accomplish the objectives listed for the project. Maintaining a 2 foot flame length will be required to produce the desired mortality of encroaching Pinon/Juniper as well as remove sagebrush that has grown old and decadent. Flame length will be the key prescriptive element for these operations, with rate of spread (ROS) and spotting distance being key indicators of the ability of on-site resources to maintain control of the fire. Fuel model SH7 is probably a little over-estimated for the conditions at Sheep Gulch, but is used as a \u201cvery high end\u201d prediction for the project. On the low intensity side, the outputs appear to be lower than expected based on normal live fuel moisture for spring-time green up. Desired prescription parameters for best fire behavior results would be inline closer with the high fire intensity results given above. High fire intensity parameters will better suited reducing P/J encroachment, and reduce hazardous fuel loading objectives, by sustaining high fire intensities into closed canopy and developing P/J stands. High Fire intensity should create/initiate torching in early encroachment areas and support some crown runs in late stage P/J stands (PJ-14).
